questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the more accurate way to frame the CAP theorem's forced choice?
options: Partition tolerance is a fact of distributed systems, so the real choice is between Consistency and Availability during a partition
You should always pick Consistency and Availability and simply avoid partitions
CAP only applies to relational databases, not NoSQL systems
A well-designed distributed system can guarantee all three properties at once
questions.explain: Partitions aren't optional in a distributed system, so 'pick 2 of 3' really means choosing between C and A when a partition occurs.

questions.q: What does 'Eventual consistency' in the BASE model actually guarantee?
options: That replicas will converge to the same value over time, given no new updates — not that every read is immediately up to date
That every read always returns the most recent write, instantly
That the database will never lose data under any circumstance
That consistency is guaranteed only during scheduled maintenance windows
questions.explain: Eventual consistency is a promise about convergence over time, not an instant guarantee — a genuinely different contract than relational strong consistency.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is BASE simply a 'sloppier' version of ACID?
options: No — it's a deliberate engineering tradeoff appropriate for workloads where a slightly stale read is acceptable but a failed request isn't
Yes, BASE exists purely because NoSQL vendors didn't implement ACID correctly
BASE and ACID guarantee exactly the same things, just with different names
BASE is only used by databases that don't support transactions at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames BASE as a deliberate, appropriate choice for certain workloads — not a lesser or careless standard.

questions.q: How does MongoDB's default consistency behavior compare to Cassandra's, per this lesson?
options: MongoDB leans CP by default (single primary accepts writes) while Cassandra leans AP by default, though both offer tunable consistency
MongoDB and Cassandra have identical, non-configurable consistency models
Cassandra leans CP while MongoDB leans AP
Neither database offers any way to adjust consistency behavior
questions.explain: MongoDB defaults toward consistency via a single primary with tunable read/write concerns; Cassandra defaults toward availability with tunable per-query consistency levels.

questions.q: What makes Azure Cosmos DB's approach to the C/A tradeoff distinctive, according to this lesson?
options: It exposes five named consistency levels (Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual) as an explicit, chosen setting
It only supports eventual consistency with no other options
It ignores the CAP theorem entirely since it's a Microsoft product
It requires strong consistency for every single request with no flexibility
questions.explain: Cosmos DB makes the CAP/BASE tradeoff an explicit, named, first-class configuration choice rather than an implicit default.
